lines.t: What do the volumes of truth say about unforgiveness and or holding grudges?
The volumes of truth teach that unforgiveness and holding grudges must be released, not
only by refraining from retaliation, but by letting resentment pass from the heart, praying
for those who caused the hurt, and taking responsibility for one's own words and conduct.
Their most direct instruction is, forgive them, pray for them, and let them go their
way.
1. Release resentment, even after betrayal. The letter, A right heart bridles the tongue,
and a forgiving heart absolves every hurt, bringing peace to the mind, dated August 8,
2011, addresses Timothy and his wife, as well as, all those who have ears to hear.
It begins, You have been faithful, and from your mouths you have testified of my glory.
glory. Yet I tell you, let judgment be no more upon your lips, and cause unforgiveness to pass
from your hearts. It then applies that instruction specifically to being hurt or betrayed. Beloved,
speak not one word concerning those who have hurt you, not one more word against those who
have betrayed you. Forgive them, pray for them, and let them go their way. The passage treats
treats faithfulness and unforgiveness as things that can coexist in someone who still needs
correction. Its instruction is not merely to avoid outward revenge, it calls for a change
in the heart toward the offending person. 2. Do not let another person's wrongdoing
govern your own heart and speech. The same letter continues, Beloved, love your enemies and pray for
those who betray you, and double for those who fight against you, for they have lifted up their
heel against me. Let resentment pass from your heart, and no more let your tongue cause you to
stumble on their account. For each is accountable for their own heart and the which flows from it,
even to every idle word. This is particularly relevant to holding a grudge. The emphasis
shifts from what the other person did, to what one continues to harbor and express because of it.
The letter leaves the other person accountable to their own master while calling the wounded
person to remain faithful in their own response. 3. Hurt is acknowledged, but resentment is warned
against. In Words to Live By, Part 1, Breaking Through the Barriers, says, When tears well up,
let them burst forth as a flood overflowing the dam, let them break through the barriers.
Yet understand this, let not your tears turn to anger when shed over hurt, nor let resentment
come forth, lest you strengthen the dam and build up the barriers, leading to rebellion
against the Lord, as you hold unforgiveness in your heart. The passage does not condemn tears
or deny the hurt. Instead, it contrasts letting grief come forth with allowing that hurt to harden
into resentment. It concludes by inviting the hearer to receive cleansing, rather than resist
it. 4. Forgiveness means more than saying the words. The short teaching, Forgive, also in Words
to Live By, Part 1, describes forgiveness in terms of both conduct and inward disposition.
Blessed are those who do not return evil for evil, or reviling for reviling, but rather pray for
their enemies. Blessed are those who hold no ill will in their heart toward another.
other. Indeed, blessed are all those who forgive everyone who has sinned against them.
For great shall be their reward in heaven. Taken together, these passages describe forgiveness as
refusing retaliation, praying for the offender, and releasing ill will, not simply making a verbal
declaration, while continuing to nourish the grievance. 5. Forgiveness and reconciliation
are related, but not identical in these passages. The instruction, forgive them, pray for them,
and let them go their way, does not require a renewed relationship in that passage.
It allows forgiveness to accompany letting the person go. Elsewhere, reconciliation in marriage
addresses repairing a relationship. An unyielding heart sows discord in marriage,
and stubbornness shuts the door to reconciliation. Yet the one who is first to say, I'm sorry,
is wise, diffusing any argument, and the one who is quick to forgive, heals the breach.
Thus, the volumes call for releasing resentment toward those who have wronged you,
while also commending humility, apology, and readiness to forgive,
give, where reconciliation is being pursued. Matthew chapter 6, verses 14 to 15. From the
TSOT. For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.
But if you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.
